tldr: Fill in the story form at slptransitions.com/share-your-story: the stage you started in, your setting and years, what you do now in plain words, how long it took, and one honest number. About fifteen minutes, and it becomes the proof the next SLP is searching for.

blocks.text: The next SLP wants to know what your Tuesday looks like

items.label: points on the most upvoted exit story in the forum threads I read for this course
comments under it, most of them questions
what the writer's new job paid over their SLP salary

blocks.text: The most upvoted exit story in those threads was a plain description of a new job. Eight years in acute care and a SNF, then a clinical analyst role at the same hospital system, hybrid, $10k a year more. The writer left the grind in: a second master's they say you don't need, and three years to land the job. The comments asked what the day looks like, whether there is job security, what the hospital paid, and why the writer wanted to leave.
I can publish salary bands and timelines. You can say what a Tuesday feels like in a job I've never had.
I wish more people in our field would take a shot. If you're miserable, we do have permission to switch jobs out of speech.
Put in the four things the most-read exit posts share

items.title: A plain job description
items.text: Say what you did yesterday in words your mother would understand. "What does a project manager actually do?" is a typical comment under these posts.

items.title: An honest number
items.text: Salary difference in either direction, hours, sessions you no longer do, or days at home. Honest does better than impressive.

items.title: A timeline with the grind
items.text: Months, applications sent, interviews had. A post that skips the 500 applications reads as luck.

items.title: An offer to talk
items.text: A LinkedIn link, so a reader can find you and ask the question your story didn't answer.

blocks.text: Readers at the permission-seeking stage are asking whether this is real for someone like them. A story from someone who had their caseload two years ago answers that in a way my data can't.
Name your stage, your setting and your first month

items: **The stage you started in.** Lesson 1.1 gave you five: private doubt, guilt, permission-seeking, practical panic, action. Name yours, and the sentence you were telling yourself at the time. A reader in that stage recognises it before anything else.
**Your setting and years in.** Add the caseload size if you have it.
**What the first month looked like.** The thing you were scared of, and what happened to it.

left.label: Vague
items: Medical SLP
I work in project management now
It took a while

right.label: Specific
items: Eight years, acute care and SNF
Yesterday: two meetings, a rollout plan, forty emails
[N] months, [N] applications, [N] interviews

blocks.title: If the number went down, say so
blocks.text: Six years of school SLP work to an entry-level CAD drafter job, with pay the writer called "WAYY worse", still drew 119 points and a thread of "do you ever miss it?". A story that leaves out the cut sends the next SLP into a budget built on a fiction.
Draft six answers here, then paste them into the form

blocks.title: Your story in six answers
blocks.text:
Where did you work as an SLP, and how long?
[Setting], [N] years, caseload of about [N].

What made you start looking?
I was at the [stage] stage. The sentence in my head was "[what you told yourself]".

What does a normal week look like now?
[Title] at [kind of company]. Yesterday I [three things you did, no acronyms].

How long did it take?
[N] months from the first serious search to the offer. About [N] applications and [N] interviews.

What was harder, or different, than you expected?
The first month: [the thing you were scared of, and what happened to it].

How does your pay compare?
[+ or - $N a year, or N hours a week, or N sessions a day I no longer do].

And for the SLP sitting where you used to sit: [the one thing you wish someone had told you].

items: Open slptransitions.com/share-your-story. The About page links to it.
Paste your draft under the matching questions. Only your first name, email, new job title and consent are required, so skip what you like.
Send the first draft. It comes straight to me, and you see the article draft before anything is published.
Say so in the last box if you'd rather talk than type, and we'll record it as a conversation instead.

items.q: Your new job pays less than your last SLP job did. What goes in your story?
options: Leave pay out and write about the hours instead
Say that it went down, and by roughly how much
Call it "about the same" so nobody is put off
items.why: A story that leaves out the cut sends the next SLP into a budget built on a fiction, and the pay-cut stories get read too.

items.q: You're now a customer success manager. Which line tells a reader the most?
options: "I manage a portfolio of accounts across the full customer lifecycle."
"Yesterday I trained a clinic's front desk on our scheduling tool and answered about forty emails."
"It's a lot like therapy, with customers in place of patients."
items.why: Readers ask what the job actually involves, and yesterday in plain words answers that where a title can't.

tldr: Three clinical habits make you good in the first ninety days, and two will hold you back. Bank one visible win by day sixty. A year in, look at the rung above the job you took: the one second move we can document paid +$10k and then +$15k.

blocks.text: Three clinical habits make you strong from the first week

items.title: Documentation
items.text: You write things down as a reflex, and many teams don't. Your notes become the record people ask for.

items.title: Reading a room
items.text: Years of IEP meetings taught you to spot the person who hasn't spoken and the one who has already decided.

items.title: Working without supervision
items.text: You've managed your own caseload, calendar and priorities for years. You already know how to work without being told each step.

blocks.text: It was a huge mentality shift for me because most roles don't completely throw you into the deep end, like I was as an SLP.
Drop two habits that come from being the expert in the room

left.label: Clinic habit
items: Answer thoroughly, because in therapy thoroughness is care.
Wait for the referral, the assignment or the required timeline.

right.label: New job
items: Say the conclusion, then stop.
Notice the gap, ask around, and bring a proposal.

blocks.text: Over-explaining and waiting to be told are the two habits to drop. In a business meeting, a three-minute answer to a one-minute question reads as uncertainty. Most non-clinical roles also expect you to notice a gap and fill it. Once you've asked around, bring your manager a problem nobody assigned you, with a proposal attached.
Spend the first ninety days asking, fixing one thing and banking a win

items: **Weeks one and two: ask before you perform.** Meet everyone your work touches and ask each of them what would make their month easier. Write it all down.
**Weeks three to five: find the small broken thing.** Pick one process people complain about and nobody owns. Check with your manager that it's yours to touch, then fix it.
**Weeks six to nine: bank the visible win by day sixty.** Choose something with a before and after that your manager can repeat to their manager. Your first review is made of this.
**Weeks ten to twelve: ask how you're doing.** Ask your manager for a ninety-day conversation if nobody schedules one, and bring the win.
**Throughout: keep a file.** Save every number, every thank-you and every problem you solved. You'll need it at your first review and again for the next job.

blocks.title: Get three dates in your first week
blocks.text: Ask whether there is an introductory or probationary period and when its review falls. Ask when the raise cycle runs and whether someone hired on your date is in the first one, because recent hires are often prorated or left out. Then put your own ASHA and state licence renewal dates in the calendar. Lesson 5.5 covers whether to keep them.

blocks.title: On imposter feelings
blocks.text: They tend to arrive once the novelty fades and you notice everyone else knows the acronyms. Two things are true at once: you are behind on the domain, and you were hired for judgement that takes years to build. The acronyms come much faster than the judgement did.
You may also miss a patient or a student at some point in the first year. That means you cared about the work, which made you good at it and will make you good at this.
A year in, look at the rung above the job you took

Around the one-year mark, the ladder starts to matter more than the job you took to get out. In clinical work the tenth year can look like the first, with the same caseload, the same productivity target and an annual review that changes little. One SLP on r/SLPcareertransitions said non-clinical jobs have a ladder, while SLP has "only lateral moves for the next 30 years."
not be too picky with your first non-clinical role. It doesn't have to be your forever job - just a pivot role
One documented second move paid +$10k, then +$15k

blocks.title: One SLP's moves, starting from a study coordinator job

items.label: study coordinator to pharma patient safety, then the next move 18 months later
study coordinator, the one path in this course where a pay cut is expected

blocks.text: The study coordinator pay cut worked as a springboard for this SLP. The other ladders in the file sit inside the first job or one rung above the entry door.

items.title: Hospital data analyst
items.text: Started at the same salary as their last SLP job, $15k below their peak home-health year, with guaranteed annual raises and "85k+" after the entry level.

items.title: Marketing
items.text: A year of applications, then: "I actually got a raise and bonus this year, whereas in my 5 years in healthcare I was given a .35 cent raise."

items.title: Project management
items.text: One SLP was an associate project manager after one year. Another landed a six-figure IT project manager role as a first move, after a fifteen-month transition.

items.title: Customer success
items.text: The entry doors are implementation specialist and onboarding manager. Customer success manager is the rung above them.

blocks.text: The rehab management rung pays, and you'd be managing what you left

If you kept one foot in a clinical setting, or took a liaison or clinical educator role at a rehab company, the ladder under you is rehab management. It usually starts as an internal promotion, program or clinical manager first and director later, and Encompass, Select Medical, Lifepoint, Sanford and Reliant all run it. The cost is on-call accountability and census pressure, which is productivity pressure wearing a manager's badge.
Give the first role a year, then watch for these signals

My honest view is that the first role deserves a year, unless it fails the bad-workplace test from lesson 0.3. Retention doubt was the first thing interviewers screened you for in lesson 6.1, and a second short stint hands that doubt to the next interviewer. In the one sequence we can document, each move came about eighteen months after the last.

left.label: Move when
items: The job stopped teaching you, and you can describe the roles above you in detail.
The posting for the rung above reads like your current week.
The next rung's documented band sits clearly above your pay, and raises come only at annual review.

right.label: Stay when
items: The only reason is that work feels quieter than a caseload. Quiet is what you paid for.
The move is for a title alone: same pay, and a second short stint to explain.

blocks.text: One transitioner "liked being entry level because it gave me time to learn about the different roles." Once you can describe those roles in detail, that phase is over.

items: Pull two postings for the rung above yours when you reach the one-year mark.
Mark every requirement line you have evidence for from the last month. If that is most of them, you're already doing the job at the lower title.
Take the unmarked lines to your next one-on-one, as the things you want to be doing by this time next year.

items.q: It's your second week. In a team meeting you notice a reporting process everyone complains about. What do you do first?
options: Rebuild it over the weekend and present the new version on Monday
Ask the people it touches what makes it painful, write it down, and ask your manager whether it's yours to fix
Say nothing until someone assigns it to you
items.why: Weeks one and two are for asking, and waiting to be assigned is one of the two clinical habits to drop.

items.q: Ten months in, a recruiter offers the same pay at another company with "Senior" in the title. Your job is still teaching you. What do you do?
options: Take it, because a senior title speeds up the move after that
Stay, and take the posting for the rung above to your next one-on-one
Take it if the new team sounds calmer
items.why: A title-only move leaves the pay the same and hands the next interviewer a second short stint to ask about.

blocks.label: Your visible win by day sixty
blocks.prompt: In the job you're aiming at, what visible win could you bank by day sixty?

takeaways: Documentation, reading a room and working unsupervised are three habits that make clinicians strong in a first non-clinical job.
Over-explaining and waiting to be assigned work are the two habits to drop.
Bank a visible win by day sixty, keep a file of numbers and thank-yous from day one, and ask in week one when reviews and raises happen.
The one second move we can document paid +$10k and then +$15k, and the study-coordinator pay cut worked as a springboard.
Move when the posting for the next rung reads like your current week, and stay put if the reason is quiet or a title.

tldr: In lesson 3.3 you sent three messages knowing that roughly one ask in four or five never gets an answer. Someone starting out will send that message to you. Ten minutes from you answers the question I can't: whether this is real for someone like them.

blocks.text: Someone starting out will send you the message you once sent

Someone at the lesson 3.3 stage will write to you, or find your LinkedIn headline and wonder whether you'd mind. We told you then to expect silence from roughly one ask in four or five, and the number never made the silence feel smaller. If one of your three messages went unanswered, you remember which one.
Your reply answers what a salary table can't

blocks.title: What they ask, and what to send

left.label: They ask
items: "What does a project manager actually do?"
"How much do you make?"
"How?"

right.label: You send
items: Yesterday in three sentences, with no acronyms and no job title.
One number you're comfortable sharing. A range counts.
Months, applications and interviews, and your résumé if you're willing.

blocks.text: A person who had a caseload two years ago answers these questions in a paragraph, and a salary table answers none of them. The most-read exit posts in the forums ended with an offer to DM, and one project-management thread drew more than twenty requests for the writer's résumé. "Do you ever miss it?" sits under those posts too.

You also know the stage the person writing to you is in. Someone at practical panic writes "I feel dumb when I look at other jobs." Someone at permission-seeking writes "Has anyone left the field and regretted it?" Whatever they typed, the question underneath is whether this is real for someone like them, and you are the evidence.
Answer in ten minutes, and send it before it's polished

items: Read the message twice and find the question underneath it.

Describe yesterday in three sentences, with no acronyms and no job title. "Two meetings, a rollout plan, forty emails" tells them more than the title does. Leave out client names and anything your employer treats as confidential.
Give one number you're comfortable sharing. A range counts. "About what I made in my best SLP year" counts.
Say how long it took and how many: months, applications, interviews. Leave the grind in, because it's what makes the rest believable.
Offer one next thing: a posting, a name, twenty minutes on a call, or your résumé with your address and phone number taken off. After "how?", the résumé is what readers of exit posts ask for most.
Send it before it's polished. A reply today does more than a perfect one next month.

blocks.title: A reply that takes ten minutes
blocks.text:
Hi [name], thanks for writing, and yes, this is real.

Quick version: I was a [setting] SLP for [N] years, and I'm now [plain-language job] at [kind of company]. Yesterday I [three things you did]. The move took [N] months and about [N] applications, and the first month was [one honest sentence].

Pay-wise I'm [a range, or how it compares to your SLP pay].

If it helps, I can [send my résumé / point you to a posting / do twenty minutes on a call next week]. What's the one thing you're most stuck on?
You don't owe anyone a mentorship. One reply, one time, is the whole action. You're giving them what you wanted a year ago: proof, from someone with your old job, that the door opens.

items.q: A school SLP you've never met writes: "Has anyone left the field and regretted it?" You have ten minutes tonight. What do you send?
options: A link to a salary table and a list of courses
Yesterday in three sentences, one number, how long it took, and one next thing
Nothing tonight. Wait for the weekend, when you can write a proper answer
items.why: The question underneath is whether this is real for someone like them, and a reply today does more than a perfect one next month.

items.q: They ask what you earn, and you'd rather not give the exact figure. What do you write?
options: Nothing about pay, and answer the other questions
A range, or how it compares with your best SLP year
That pay shouldn't be the reason to leave
items.why: A range counts, and an honest number is one of the four things the most-read exit posts share.

action.label: I answered one
action.prompt: Find one message from an SLP earlier in this program, or one that has been sitting in your LinkedIn inbox, and answer it with the six steps above: yesterday in three sentences, one number, the timeline with the grind left in, and one next thing. Ten minutes, then send.

takeaways: Roughly one informational-interview ask in four or five never gets an answer, which is why one reply from you matters.
The questions under exit posts are small: what the day is, what it pays, whether you miss it.
Answer in ten minutes with yesterday in three sentences, one number, the timeline, and one next thing.
After "how?", the résumé is what readers ask for most, so send yours if you're willing.
One reply, one time, is the whole action.
